The Unavoidable Truth: Intel prioritized high-margin enterprise AI chips over budget consumer silicon.

The Unavoidable Lie: Consumer PC scarcity is driven purely by unexpected market demand and memory shortages.

Alethekanon:
Financial records expose the discrepancy between PR claims and manufacturing priority. When server revenue surges 78% while PC sales contract 5%, scarcity is an operational choice rather than an unavoidable physical limit.

Everyday students and families needing basic laptops are left paying higher prices for stripped-down devices, while corporate giants pretend their hands are tied.

Classic tech PR pivot. They tell us budget chips are 'sold out' like hot concert tickets, but really they just moved all the factory lines to make AI chips for big tech.

Intel’s CFO says it’s ‘not optimistic about next year in terms of memory.’﻿

Intel’s CFO says it’s ‘not optimistic about next year in terms of memory.’﻿

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

See All by Stevie Bonifield

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

See All by Stevie Bonifield

During Intel’s latest earnings call, CEO Lip-Bu Tan said that demand for its budget-focused Wildcat Lake chips “is outstripping supply.” According to CFO David Zinsner, the chips are now sold out. Zinsner said Intel has “seen significant growth in Wildcat Lake. It’s coming exactly at the right time because it’s cost-optimized and we’re seeing a lot of focus in that regard.”

As shortages of RAM and other components have driven up PC prices over recent months, Intel’s Wildcat Lake chips have been appearing in new lower-cost Windows laptops on par with the MacBook Neo, like the new Dell XPS 13 or the HP Omnibook 5 14. Wildcat Lake laptops like these have budget-friendly starting prices, but often with just 8GB of RAM, which Windows laptops can struggle to get by on.

Intel doesn’t expect the memory shortage to improve any time soon. Zinsner responded to a question about memory supply, saying, “Make no mistake, we are not optimistic about next year in terms of memory.” He added, “we’ll, you know, have to see in ‘28 whether things improve, but our expectation is that it does not improve in ‘27.” That’s more optimistic than SK Hynix’s prediction that the RAM shortage will drag on through 2030.

Tan also acknowledged the PC demand slowdown, saying, “The industry continues to navigate one of the most significant supply shortages in the [sic] history, driven by the unprecedented demand for super intelligence,” referring to AI. Zinsner went on to respond to a question during the earnings call, saying, “We do think the PC is going to go through a renaissance despite this.”

Schoolgirl, 8, selling chocolate crackles to help the homeless has stall shut down by bureaucrats in permit row

An eight-year-old's dream of running her own cake stall was left in tatters after she was ordered to shut down the small kiosk over a missing permit.

Actual Article Body:
By ANTOINETTE MILIENOS, NEWS REPORTER, AUSTRALIA

Published:  12:03 AEDT, 30 October 2026   |  Updated:  12:22 AEDT, 30 October 2026

An eight-year-old's dream of running her own cake stall was left in tatters after she was ordered to shut down the small kiosk over a missing permit.

Western Australian mother Kim Macdonald helped her daughter Mischa fulfil what she described as her dream of opening a makeshift stall.

Mischa's stand, set up at Perth's Hyde Park on a weekend earlier in October, sold her homemade chocolate crackles, cups of cordial and artwork she had created herself.

She displayed a sign telling customers that a portion of earnings from the two dozen sweets she sold would go to people who are experiencing homelessness.

But Mischa's dreams were 'momentarily crushed' when she was asked to present documentation.

'While we sought permission from the delightful owner of the Hyde Park kiosk before selling her two dozen sweet treats, it never occurred to me that she would require an official permit,' Mrs Macdonald wrote in an opinion piece for The West Australian.

'That point was hammered home by an official from a stage show at the park that day, who demanded to see a permit before brusquely shutting her down, warning the breach risked having the entire event cancelled.

'Watching it get closed down by bureaucrats because she did not have a permit is one of [the] more frustrating experiences.'

A Perth mother has revealed how her eight-year-old's dream of running a cake stall was crushed after she was forced to shut down due to a missing permit

Mrs Macdonald said her daughter was inundated with support from visitors and locals who were confused by the 'heavy-handed rebuke'.

Before the closure, Mischa had sold the chocolate crackles for about $1, as well as 50¢ cups of cordial, paper chains and cat pictures drawn on Bunnings paint swatches.

She accepted payments using an electronic card reader, which Mrs Macdonald said allowed her daughter to open her first bank account and learn how money moves.

Mrs Macdonald said Mischa's confidence grew as customers bought her goods.

The mother said she was not only frustrated by the situation, but believed permit requirements could discourage entrepreneurial thinking.

'It points to a potential change in our national character, with Australia at risk of becoming so overregulated, sanitised and risk-averse that there is no tolerance for initiative,' she wrote in her column.

'Encouraging an entrepreneurial mindset in the next generation should be a national priority, given Australia is currently suffering low productivity growth and weakening business dynamism.'

Mrs Macdonald said her daughter was not alone, claiming many children and charities had seen their endeavours shut down because of permit issues.

While she noted her daughter was addressed by an event organiser, she claimed councils are usually the ones calling the shots on permits.

She said bureaucracy, such as permits, was discouraging children from developing initiative and business skills.

'Let children learn to run a business before bureaucracy teaches them not to bother,' she added.
